headline: Paraguay fired its president. He's under arrest.
summary: Paraguay's Senate voted 44-0 on Friday to remove President Santiago Peña, three days after regulators seized Ueno Bank and froze nearly 3 million customers' savings. He had offered to resign. Senators impeached him instead, which strips his immunity. Prosecutors ordered his arrest and questioned him Saturday. He denies wrongdoing.

cover_question.q: Why not just let him resign?

cover_answer: Resigning kept his immunity. Removal took it away.
table_question: If you quit before you're fired, should the trouble end there?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In a country called Paraguay, a big bank broke, and about 3 million people couldn't get their money out, like a vending machine that eats your coins. People blamed the president, so the leaders voted to take his job away, and police took him in for questions. The grown-ups are working on paying everyone back.
5-7.why: The vending machine is the whole bank. At this age the stuck money is the story, and 'they're paying people back' is the landing.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from the object in front of them, so the bank is a vending machine that ate the coins: money went in, nothing came out, and grown-ups are working on getting it back. The arrest stays short and calm: this child reads your face before your words. Expect "could our bank do that?" Say what is true for you.

8-12.script: Ueno Bank in Paraguay had nearly 3 million customers. Regulators seized it Tuesday and froze their money. Lawmakers say President Peña steered public money into it. Friday the Senate voted 44-0 to remove him, and prosecutors ordered his arrest. The referee sent off the captain.
8-12.why: Seizure, freeze, vote, arrest: a chain, and the captain answers. At 12 fairness is the question, and the sent-off captain is a rule they know.
8-12.why_long: A twelve-year-old is working out whether the rules apply to the people at the top, so the script runs the chain: the bank seized, the money frozen, the 44-0 vote, the arrest. The referee sending off the captain is a rule they know. Expect "did he steal it?" Nobody has proved that. He denies it, and prosecutors have only started.

13-17.script: Peña offered to resign. The Senate refused and removed him 44-0: quit and you keep your immunity, get impeached and you lose it. Should quitting end it? Second: the bank held 3 million people's savings in a country of 6 million, and he had shares in its owner until last year. Who was watching?
13-17.why: Resigning and removal empty the same chair and end differently. At 14 they can hold both and argue which should win.
13-17.why_long: A fourteen-year-old can hold two true things at once: he left either way, and how he left decides whether he can be prosecuted. The script gives them that gap, then widens it to oversight, a question with no villain. Expect "will he go to prison?" Nobody knows. He denies it, and prosecutors are investigating breach of trust.

5-7.q: Will the people get their money back?
5-7.a: Some already have. About 1.2 million people got money back so far.

8-12.q: Did the president steal the money?
8-12.a: Nobody has proved that. Lawmakers accuse him; he denies it.

8-12.q: Why did his own party vote against him?
8-12.a: Everyone did: 44-0. Half the country couldn't reach its savings.

13-17.q: Why not just let him resign?
13-17.a: Quitting kept his immunity. Impeachment took it away.

13-17.q: How does one bank get half a country?
13-17.a: It grew fast, and lawmakers say public money was steered into it.
